title: Biggest Lottery Winners: What Happened After They Won
description: The jaw-dropping truth about America's biggest lottery winners isn't the jackpot — it's what came next. Real stories, real people, real consequences.
content:
The Day Everything Changed

Before the press conferences, before the financial advisors, before the relatives who suddenly remembered your birthday — there was just a moment. A quiet, ordinary moment that split a life in two: before and after. For some of America's biggest lottery winners, that moment happened in a gas station parking lot. For others, it came at a kitchen table at midnight, squinting at a phone screen and not quite believing what they were reading. The numbers matched. Everything else would have to wait.

What makes these stories worth telling isn't the size of the checks. It's what the people did in the minutes, hours, and years that followed — decisions made under impossible pressure, with no manual and no rehearsal. Some of those decisions were wise. Some were heartbreaking. Most were simply human.

Who Were These People Before the Win

A Hospital Worker, a Young Man, and a Mystery

Mavis Wanczyk had spent 32 years working at Mercy Medical Center in Springfield, Massachusetts. She was a mother, a grandmother, a woman who showed up for her shift and did her job. By the summer of 2017, she had been buying lottery tickets for years — not obsessively, just the way a lot of people do, with a quiet, persistent hope that maybe someday the numbers would line up. On the evening of August 23, 2017, they did.

Manuel Franco was 24 years old and living in New Berlin, Wisconsin, when he stopped at a local store in March 2019. He worked a regular job. He was, by every public account, an ordinary young man — the kind of person who might not have made the news at all if the universe hadn't intervened with a string of impossible digits printed on a slip of paper.

Edwin Castro is, in some ways, the most fascinating figure in American lottery history — not because of what he said, but because of how little he said. A California man who claimed his prize through a trust in November 2022, Castro has remained almost entirely out of the public eye since his win. What we know is documented. What we don't know is, perhaps, the point.

The Moment of the Claim — Decisions Made in Hours That Lasted a Lifetime

The Phone Call That Said It All

When Mavis Wanczyk walked into the Massachusetts State Lottery office to claim her $758.7 million Powerball jackpot, she did something before she even left the building: she called her employer and quit. Not dramatically, not with a speech — just a phone call, clean and final. Thirty-two years of shifts, and she was done. She chose the lump sum option, which after federal and state taxes left her with a payout that, while still life-altering, was a fraction of the advertised figure. She told reporters she planned to "take care of her family and just be."

The claim process itself is deceptively simple and profoundly consequential. Winners typically have between 90 days and a year, depending on the state, to come forward. In that window, they must decide whether to take the annuity — paid out over 29 years for Powerball — or the lump sum, which is roughly half the advertised jackpot before taxes. That decision, made under acute emotional stress and public scrutiny, shapes everything that follows. For those unfamiliar with how dramatically taxes reduce the actual payout, the numbers can be startling. See how they break down with our lottery tax calculator.

A Scream Heard by the Neighbors

Manuel Franco reportedly said he was so overwhelmed when he realized he'd won the $768.4 million Powerball jackpot that he screamed — and his neighbors called to check on him. That image, more than any press conference photo, captures what this moment actually feels like. He was 24. He had no roadmap. He took the lump sum, which came to roughly $477 million before taxes, and stepped into a spotlight he hadn't asked for and quickly stepped back out of.

The Most Human Moment

"I just want to spend time with my family. I've been working since I was 14 years old, and now I'm going to take care of them." — Mavis Wanczyk, at her August 2017 press conference following her $758.7 million Powerball win.

That statement — straightforward, unheroic, completely believable — is what separates these stories from fables. She wasn't talking about yachts or mansions. She was talking about rest, and about the people she loved. It was the most ordinary thing imaginable, said by a woman standing in front of cameras holding a check with nine figures on it.

The Long Game — What the Money Did and Didn't Do

When Privacy Becomes the Prize

Edwin Castro's win on November 8, 2022, produced the largest lottery jackpot in verified American history: $2.04 billion. He claimed through a trust — a legal structure that, in California, still required his name to be made public — and then, as far as the public record shows, went quiet. No interviews. No foundation announcements. No tabloid sightings. For Castro, the most valuable thing that money may have bought was the ability to disappear from the story entirely.

That choice stands in sharp contrast to Jack Whittaker, who won $314.9 million in Powerball on Christmas Day 2002 in West Virginia and immediately became one of the most publicly chronicled lottery winners in history — though not for reasons he would have chosen. Already a successful businessman at the time of his win, Whittaker gave generously to charity, but the years that followed brought a cascade of documented legal troubles, personal losses, and public hardships that he himself attributed, at least in part, to the visibility and chaos the win brought into his life.

The Quiet Ones

Merle and Patricia Butler of Illinois waited months before claiming their share of a $218.6 million Mega Millions jackpot in 2012 — one of three winning tickets split in what was then a record drawing. When they finally came forward, they arrived with lawyers, financial advisors, and a plan. They were older, deliberate, and prepared. Their story rarely makes the headlines precisely because it unfolded so carefully. For information on how Illinois handles lottery claims and taxes, see the Illinois lottery guide.

Gloria MacKenzie, who was 84 years old when she claimed a $590.5 million Powerball jackpot in Florida in May 2013, became the oldest solo jackpot winner in American history. She took the lump sum. She had reportedly allowed another shopper to go ahead of her in the ticket line — a small act of courtesy that may have altered the trajectory of a life already well-lived. For Florida-specific lottery rules and winner information, visit the Florida lottery page.

Lessons Without the Lecture

It would be easy to draw a tidy moral from these stories — take the annuity, hire a lawyer, stay off social media, trust no one. But the reality is more complicated and more interesting than any checklist. What these winners share isn't a formula. It's the experience of being handed something that changes every relationship, every morning, every sense of what comes next — and having to figure out the rest alone, usually very fast.

  • Anonymity, where the law allows it, appears to offer genuine protection. States like California require winners to go public, while others permit trusts or delayed disclosure. Castro's decision to claim through a trust was legally sound and, by all appearances, personally useful.
  • The lump sum vs. annuity decision is permanent. Most documented winners chose the lump sum, accepting a significantly smaller immediate payout in exchange for certainty. Neither option is wrong, but neither can be undone.
  • The people who planned before claiming — like the Butlers — tended to navigate the transition more smoothly. Waiting a few weeks to assemble legal and financial counsel, even when it felt excruciating, appears to have served them well.
  • The money itself is neutral. What it amplifies — generosity, isolation, impulsiveness, grief, purpose — was already there. These stories, at their core, are not about lottery jackpots. They're about character under pressure.
